source_text: Ubi hic ergo accusatur natura? Ubi humanae substantiae culpantur exordia? Ubi motus generantis arguitur? Luce clarius est, quod sola a Magistro Gentium conveniatur voluntas, ut abdicet occulta dedecoris [n383] et in meliorem vitam actuum correctione proficiat. Sed iam accipiat expositio nostra compendium nec interpretari in his locis dicta Apostoli perseveret; ipsum de suis disserentem sensibus audiamus. In fine disputationis eius apparebit, cuius dogmati fideique consentiat. Nos nempe dicimus de peccato Apostolum voluntatis humanae, quae in unoquoque peccante est, locutum fuisse; tu vero de eo, quod Fausto credis generatione transmissum et a cunctis sine voluntate susceptum. Concertationes itaque nostrae, si placet, facessant et, ut mediocriter agam, dissimulemus Apostoli dignitatem, qua praescribi posset, etiamsi vobis per omnia eius verba concinerent, tamen illum pro officii sui splendore nihil tam deforme sensisse, ambiguitatem esse elocutionum, non sensuum pravitatem; hoc solum ei in praesenti negotio concedatur, ut vir non perturbatae mentis magis scripta sua quam tu intellexisse credatur. Non ergo regnet - inquit - peccatum in vestro mortali corpore ad oboediendum ei [n384] . Possem iam hic dicere exhortationis testimonio probatum esse de peccatis eum agere voluntatis, quia mala, si essent naturalia, per iustitiam defendi possent, per misericordiam postremo defleri, nullo autem pacto admonerentur cavenda. Quovis enim naturali malo, si ullum esse posset, hoc malum erat maius insaniae, qua tenebatur, quicumque devotionem in cavendis rebus naturalibus exigebat. Apostolus autem nihil sanxit, quod possit iure reprehendi; peccatum itaque voluntatis ostendit, quod inculcat debere vitari.
pass_a_gloss: Where here therefore is nature accused? Where are the beginnings of human substance blamed? Where is the motion of one generating accused? It is clearer than light that only will is convened by the Teacher of the Gentiles, so that it may abdicate the hidden things of disgrace and by a correction of acts may profit unto a better life. But now let our exposition take a shortcut and not persevere in interpreting the Apostle's sayings in these places; let us hear him himself discussing about his own senses. In the end of his disputation it will appear to whose dogma and faith he consents. We namely say that the Apostle spoke about a sin of human will, which is in each one sinning; but you about that which you believe with Faustus transmitted by generation and taken up by all without will. Let therefore our concertations, if it pleases, be gone, and, that I may act moderately, let us dissemble the Apostle's dignity, by which it could be prescribed, even if his words sang together with you through all things, nevertheless that he, for the splendor of his office, meant nothing so deformed, that there is an ambiguity of elocutions, not a crookedness of senses; let this alone be granted him in the present business, that a man of an unperturbed mind be believed to have understood his own writings more than you. Let not therefore, he says, sin reign in your mortal body toward obeying it. I could already here say that by a testimony of exhortation it has been proved that he acts about sins of will, because evils, if they were natural, could be defended through justice, finally be wept through mercy, but by no pact would they be warned as to be guarded against. For than any natural evil, if any could be, this evil of insanity by which he was held was greater, whoever was exacting devotion in guarding against natural things. But the Apostle sanctioned nothing which can be rightly reprehended; he showed therefore a sin of will, which he stamps in as ought to be avoided.

pass_b_english: Where here is nature accused? Where are the beginnings of human substance blamed? Where is the movement of the one begetting a child condemned? It is clearer than light that the Teacher of the Gentiles addresses only the will, so that it renounces hidden disgrace (2 Corinthians 4:2) and advances to a better life through corrected actions. But now let our explanation take a shorter course and stop continually interpreting the apostle’s words in these passages. Let us hear him discuss his own meaning. At the end of his argument it will become clear whose doctrine and faith he agrees with. We say, of course, that the apostle spoke of the sin of human will, present in each person who sins. You speak of the sin which, believing Faustus, you think was transmitted through generation and received by everyone without willing it. Let our disputes, then, cease, if you please. To proceed modestly, let us set aside the apostle’s dignity. On that ground alone we could insist that, even if his words agreed with you in every respect, he nevertheless could have intended nothing so disgraceful, given the splendor of his office: the fault would lie in ambiguous expressions, not perverse meanings. Let us grant him only this in the present matter: as a man whose mind was not disordered, he should be believed to have understood his own writings better than you do. ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey it’ (Romans 6:12). I could already say here that the exhortation proves he is treating sins of will. For if evils were natural, they could be defended on grounds of justice or, at least, lamented out of pity; but in no way could people be admonished to avoid them. Greater than any natural evil, if such an evil could exist, would be the evil of the madness possessing anyone who demanded devotion in avoiding natural things. But the apostle enacted nothing that could justly be criticized. He therefore indicates a sin of will when he insists that it must be avoided.

choices.why: Julian's target is Augustine's claim that sin is transmitted by begetting; keep generation vs imitation.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
